title: I- verb forms
summary: The prefix i- makes passive verbs for doing something for someone or using something: isúlat, ilutò, ibigáy
goals: Understand what the prefix i- adds to a word
Form the tenses of i- verbs (and the variant ipag-)
Use the three sentence patterns that turn -um- and mag- sentences into i- sentences
Learn common i- verbs and avoid the common mistakes

blocks.t: The prefix [[i-|pred]] is added to words to make **passive verbs**. It shows that something is **used** to do something. For example, add i- to the noun **sulat** (letter) and you get the verb **isulat** (*to write down something*).
When i- is added to a verb, it can also show that something is done **for someone else**, as well as doing the action of the root word on or for the subject:

blocks.title: In general
blocks.t: The meaning of an i- verb is usually **to do something for another person**.

blocks.title: Active and passive
blocks.t: In Lesson 14 you met **-um-** and **mag-** verbs, which are **active**: the subject does the action. An **i-** verb is **passive**: the subject is the thing or person the action is done to or for.

sections.title: When to use an i- verb

blocks.t: Use the i- form only when an active **-um-** or **mag-** sentence has a **direct object**: the noun or pronoun that receives the action of the verb.
To find the direct object in an -um- or mag- sentence: take the verb on its own, put *whom* (**sino**) or *what* (**ano**) after it, and make it a question.

items.tl: Bumilí ng isdâ ang babáe para sa kanyáng iná.
items.en: The woman bought fish for her mother.

blocks.title: Mostly mag- verbs
items: An i- verb is **usually** the passive form of a **mag-** verb, and **seldom** of an -um- verb.
Sometimes, instead of an i- verb, a mag- verb takes the variant **ipag-**, which means doing something for another. It normally follows the **first sentence pattern** (below).

sections.title: Forming i- verbs: roots starting with a consonant

blocks.t: For roots that begin with a **consonant**, the prefix **i-** (or its variant **ipag-**) goes on **all forms and tenses**, and the infix **-in-** is added in the **past** and **present**.

blocks.title: The variant ipag-: sulat → ipagsulát
Spot the pattern
items: Past: **-in-** goes in after the first letter: s**in**úlat, s**in**áma; with ipag-: **ip-in-ag**sulát.
Present: **-in-** plus the **first syllable repeated**: isinu**sú**lat, isina**sá**ma.
Future: just repeat the **first syllable**: isu**sú**lat, isa**sá**ma, ipagsu**su**lát.

blocks.title: Spelling
blocks.t: The book writes **isulat** for the infinitive and imperative, but **isúlat** in its list of i- verbs.

sections.title: Forming i- verbs: roots starting with a vowel or h, l, y, w

blocks.t: For roots that begin with a **vowel** or with the consonants **h, l, y** and **w**, the prefix **i-** still goes on all forms and tenses, but the infix **-in-** becomes **-ni-**, added in the **past** and **present**.

blocks.title: -in- or -ni-?
items: Root starts with a consonant (not h, l, y, w): **-in-** → is**in**úlat.
Root starts with a vowel or h, l, y, w: **-ni-** → i**ni**hánap, i**ni**lutò.

blocks.t: When the i- verb's active form uses **-um-**, the **indirect object** becomes the **subject** of the i- sentence. The indirect object is the part introduced by **sa**, **para sa**, **kay** or **para kay** (see Lesson 27).

Watch the article **ang** move: in the -um- sentence it marks the doer, but in the i- sentence it moves to **iná**, making **ang kanyáng iná** the subject. Remember (Lesson 4): **ang** and **si** introduce the subject.

items.tl: Bumilí ng isdâ ang babáe para sa kanyáng iná.
items.en: The woman bought fish for her mother.

items.tl: Ibinilí ng babáe ng isdâ ang kanyáng iná.
items.en: The woman bought fish for her mother.

items.tl: Bumása ng aklát ang gurò para kay Joe.
items.en: (The book prints "The woman bought fish for her mother" here again by mistake. Compare pattern 3 below: The teacher read the book to the child.)

items.tl: Ibinása ng gurò ng aklát si Joe.
items.en: (Same meaning as the sentence above.)

blocks.title: si for names
blocks.t: Joe is a person's name, so the i- sentence uses **si**, not **ang**. **Ang** introduces names of places and things.
When the i- verb's active form uses **mag-** (or **nag-** in the past), the **direct object** becomes the **subject** of the i- sentence, introduced by **si** or **ang**.

items.tl: Naglutò siyá ng pagkain para sa anák.
items.en: She/He cooked the food for her/his child.

items.tl: Inilutò niyá ang pagkain para sa anák.
items.en: She/He cooked the food for her/his child.

items.tl: Nag-áyos ng silíd si Benjamin.
items.en: Benjamin arranged the room.

items.tl: Iniáyos ni Benjamin ang silíd.
items.en: Benjamin arranged the room.

blocks.title: The doer changes form
items: A personal pronoun in the mag- sentence becomes a **possessive** pronoun in the i- sentence: **siyá** → **niyá**.
A person's name changes the same way: **si Benjamin** → **ni Benjamin**.

sections.title: Sentence pattern 3: -um- and mag- with the same meaning

blocks.t: When the **-um-** and **mag-** verbs have **similar meanings** (see Lesson 14), the i- verb follows the **first** sentence pattern: the indirect object becomes the subject.

items.tl: Bumása ng aklát ang gurò para sa batà.
items.en: The teacher read the book to the child.

items.tl: Nagbasá ng aklát ang gurò para sa batà.
items.en: The teacher read the book to the child.

items.tl: Ibinása ng aklát ng gurò ang batà.
items.en: The teacher read the book to the child.

blocks.title: The three patterns
items: **1. From -um-:** the indirect object (sa, para sa, kay, para kay) becomes the subject.
**2. From mag-:** the direct object becomes the subject; siyá → niyá, si → ni.
**3. -um- and mag- mean the same:** follow pattern 1.

items.tl: Ibinilí ako ng baró ng áking iná.
items.en: Bought for me a dress by my mother. (literal) / My mother bought a dress for me.

items.tl: Ibíbilád ko ang sapátos.
items.en: Will put under the sun by me the shoes. (literal) / I shall put the shoes under the sun.

items.en: Thrown away by him/her the stale bread. (literal) / He threw away the stale bread.

blocks.title: Look closely
items: The doer is shown with **ko, mo, niyá** or **ni / ng**, and the thing acted on takes **ang**.
Many literal translations sound odd in English, so the book also gives a natural one.
This lesson writes **baró** (dress); Lesson 4 wrote **barò**.

blocks.title: Don't use -in on these roots
blocks.t: With these roots, do not add **-in** (balitain, tapunin…). Put **i-** in front instead, and add the infix for the past: **ibinalík**, **itinápon**, **isinará**.
The book asks you to **pick out the i- verb** you would need, and translate each sentence into Tagalog. It prints no answers; use the lists and patterns above.

blocks.title: Translate into Tagalog
More practice from the book
items: Make your own sentences with the other i- verbs in the list.
Change your i- sentences back into **mag-** or **-um-** sentences using the three patterns. The subject of the i- sentence becomes the direct or indirect object.
Say the different tense forms of as many i- verbs as you can, out loud.

blocks.title: Remember
items: i- makes passive verbs; it usually means doing something for another person.
Consonant roots: -in- in past and present (isinúlat, isinusúlat). Vowel or h, l, y, w roots: -ni- (inihánap, inilutò).
Future: repeat the first syllable (isusúlat, ihahánap).
Pattern 1 (-um-): indirect object → subject. Pattern 2 (mag-): direct object → subject. Pattern 3: like pattern 1.
Say ibalík, itápon, isará, not balikin, tapunin, sarahin.

exercises.q: What does the prefix i- usually add to a verb's meaning?
options: to do something for another person
to be able to do something
exercises.answer: to do something for another person

exercises.q: Is an i- verb active or passive?
exercises.explain: The prefix i- forms passive verbs.

recap: The prefix i- makes passive verbs, usually meaning to do something for another person.
Use an i- verb only when the -um- or mag- sentence has a direct object.
Consonant roots: isulat, isinúlat, isinusúlat, isusúlat. Vowel or h, l, y, w roots: ihánap, inihánap, inihahánap, ihahánap.
Pattern 1 (-um-): indirect object → subject. Pattern 2 (mag-): direct object → subject, siyá → niyá. Pattern 3: like pattern 1.
Say ibalità, ihúlog, itaním, ibalík, isará; not balitain, hulugin, tanimin, balikin, sarahin.
